extracted.intended_audience: students and novice mathematicians learning composition and mathematical writing
extracted.subtask_description: A handout / lecture notes describing composition exercises and style rules aimed at improving general prose and mathematical writing (techniques, drills, and editorial guidance). Useful for novice writers in mathematics and related disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphatic positions
rubrics_metrics.description: The front of the sentence and the back are the emphatic positions ("The middle of a sentence is sort of a slum.").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence placement of emphasis by writing sentences that stress different parts; discover emphasis patterns by practice rather than taking authority's word for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write nonsense exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a completely unrelated stream of thoughts with the correct glue: words like "thus," "therefore," and "as we can see."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reveals how connectives and discourse markers create the appearance of logical flow; recommended as a playful exercise (Mary-Claire calls it "incredibly wonderful").

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual labor / copying as close reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Use manual copying (pen, pencil, crayon, left hand, right hand, typewriter, word-processor) to slow the brain and gain insight into the passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy passages you like, dislike, find difficult, etc., to learn different things; manual transcription helps close reading and composition skill-building; memorization and recitation also useful (Auden: copy on a typewriter to show contempt; longhand to show admiration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose anywhere (avoid ritual restrictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't impose rigid restrictions on how or where you compose (e.g., "I can only write on yellow pads with a fountain pen").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be able to compose on a cocktail napkin; flexibility trains real composing habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aloud and peer listening
rubrics_metrics.description: Read your own writing aloud and form partnerships to read and listen to each other's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud reveals cadence and tone; listening to others' readings is revealing; use sparingly—too much critique can fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks on paper / revision mindset
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing is forgiving: you can work on it until you get it right. Use writing to discover your meaning ("How do I know what I mean till I see what I say?").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat writing as a medium that can be iterated until clarity and precision emerge; don't expect perfect first drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggerate defects to find voice (stance/voice/tone technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Borrow speech-therapist technique: exaggerate defects until you understand what characterizes them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If someone called you 'breezy', try writing something truly off the wall to understand the characteristic; exaggeration helps identify and control tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use discipline-provided 'glue' for technical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation, invention, and similar creative exercises are less crucial for technical writers because the discipline provides structural glue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus creative exercises where they serve your discipline; exploit disciplinary conventions rather than inventing glue from scratch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scansion / verse-writing to improve prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse-writing (scansion) is hard but important; writing verse helps other composition skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write verse honoring conventional rhyme and stress to gain benefit; treating verse-writing like weightlifting for composition; trust that verse helps clarity in mathematical exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precis / reduction exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing a passage's word count (5%, 25%, 50%, etc.) without changing meaning teaches concision; abstracting content into a short summary (<=10 sentences) clarifies structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At some reduction threshold you must change structure; never change essential meaning though some details will be dispensable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nearly-real drafting exercises (flip/replace/crunch/unpack/etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises that mimic real writing tasks: flip sentence order, change pace, write without adjectives/adverbs, unpack metaphors, define common words, exemplify abstract nouns, rewrite instructions for novices, write jokes, translate unknown languages, Ben Franklin's reconstruction exercise, sustained 'push' freewriting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These drills simulate practical writing challenges and train adaptability; Ben Franklin exercise: reduce to one- and two-word hints, jumble, reconstruct, compare to original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary: Replace
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a long passage and replace at least three words in every sentence with synonyms keeping the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaches sensitivity to diction and nuance; helps notice connotations and precise signification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary: Multiply (thesaurus entry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a word and write a thesaurus entry listing words at every level of diction that mean approximately the same thing; compare to real thesaurus entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improves awareness of register and diction choices; maintain good dictionaries and at least one thesaurus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax: Transform sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform every sentence in a multi-page passage so it says approximately the same thing in different syntax, changing vocabulary as little as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build facility with alternative syntactic shapes and discover different emphases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax: Build tight parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: Write sentences containing tight parallels—pairs of structures that match perfectly in number and kind, including subordinate structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push yourself to write long parallel members (15–20 words) until every grammatical and physical end coincides; practices rhythm and balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax: Rewrite as periodic sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite a non-periodic sentence (or pair) as a periodic sentence where grammatical and physical ends coincide and predicate comes at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices suspense-building and control of clause placement; try whole paragraphs in periodic sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax: Emphasize different points
rubrics_metrics.description: Recast a sentence to express the same meaning but emphasize a different point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train shifting emphasis by syntactic reordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frozen sounds: Transcription
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcribe five minutes of recorded radio/news/public conversation/lecture/TV dialog to gain awareness of natural speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop ear for ordinary phrasing and extemporaneous cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frozen sounds: Read/listen and mutter
rubrics_metrics.description: Read aloud a page of your writing and have others read it; learn to mutter what you're writing as a check on cadence and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud is an efficient way to check rhythm and tone; it exposes unnatural diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks on paper: Close-eyes composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose a paragraph with eyes shut; start over fresh without peeking to force reliance on memory/voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use blind composition to test internalized structure and flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks on paper: Tabulate and caption exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn linked conditionals into a table; write captions that fit picture underlines exactly (one-line, two-line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exercises teach alternative organization and compression of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stance/voice/tone drills (change stance, take both sides, hyperbolize, euphemize, obfuscate, pontificate, vacillate, strengthen/vitiate, change tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple rewrites aimed at altering stance, point-of-view, tone, or rhetorical strategy (e.g., rewrite a textbook explanation as a personal letter; write pros/cons arguments; describe plainly vs. euphemistically; make prose obscure; make an author pompous; inject doubts; strengthen/weaken passages; remove sarcasm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These show how diction and structural choices create different rhetorical effects; useful for adapting to audiences and understanding tone control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation: expand/contract/rethink/sensualize/Agassiz exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises to alter scale (expand a paragraph to five pages and then condense), to describe only by appearance or sounds, to present sensory-focused descriptions, or daily repeated careful description of the same object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trains attention to detail and perceptual description; expands descriptive resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same as and different from: compare/analogize/differentiate
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises in comparison and analogy: choose unlike things and write similes explaining similarities; invent analogies to explain concepts to different audiences; differentiate similar words with short definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaches making instructive analogies and precise lexical distinctions useful for exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention: combine/categorize
rubrics_metrics.description: Random-word combination sentences and categorization of random nouns into schemes, with explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trains ideation and classification habits useful for conceptual invention in a discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scansion exercises: render prose as verse and change meter
rubrics_metrics.description: Render newspaper stories, recipes, or expository passages into specified verse forms (couplets, ballads, villanelles, sonnets); change meter (tetrameter to pentameter), or write daily sonnets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verse exercises strengthen control of rhythm and prosody; honor conventional rhyme/stress to gain the benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tropes / rhetorical-figure practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Write examples for every rhetorical figure listed in a handbook (e.g., Unham's list) rather than only thinking about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producing examples is more beneficial than theoretical familiarity; avoid shallow engagement by actual practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ben Franklin reconstruction exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce a passage to one- and two-word hints on separate slips, jumble them, wait weeks, then reconstruct and compare to original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests memory, structure recognition, and what constitutes essential content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Push (timed freewriting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write sentences at a deliberate pace for five minutes without repeating yourself, producing nonsense allowed; increase gradually to twenty minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Builds fluency and reduces inhibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of reader background and define basic terms early
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask what background readers share and define terms clearly at the start (especially in graph theory where terminology varies—e.g., path vs. simple path vs. walk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming inconsistent conventions across authors; define even basic symbols/terminology if they might be unfamiliar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be succinct: "Less is more."
rubrics_metrics.description: Condense lengthy multi-part definitions or expressions when possible; shorten intimidating definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shorter, clearer definitions aid readability; remove unused symbols like W2 if unused elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of terms (especially among coauthors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use consistent names for the same concept (avoid coauthors calling the same thing 'dominators' and 'parents').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide on common terminology early; inconsistent naming confuses readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't define unused terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid defining terms that never appear later in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defining unused notation needlessly burdens the reader (Feynman's complaint about premature symbols).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense and factual statements in mathematical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate tenses for timeless facts (algorithms have shown ... not 'had'); the object of 'had' vs 'have' depends on whether you refer to algorithms or problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match tense to the timelessness of mathematical facts and clarity of reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation formatting and parenthetical references
rubrics_metrics.description: References should be parenthetical so sentences remain readable without them; keep spacing before brackets; avoid awkward inline citations like 'Tarjan[Gab83]'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use citation styles that don't break sentence flow; consider numbered references or automated systems (TeX/BibTeX) to avoid global edits when inserting refs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commas: put where a speaker would pause
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid too many commas; as a rough guide, place a comma where a speaker would pause to draw breath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: remove unnecessary commas around variable names in expressions; use commas to reflect natural cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous words and awkward overloading (e.g., 'left')
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful when idioms conflict with other senses of words; ambiguity arises when the same word has competing technical and ordinary senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rephrase or choose alternative words to avoid confusion (e.g., 'the node J is left' ambiguous between direction and past tense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pluralizing symbols and genitive forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard plural of a symbol like Hi is 'the Hi's' can conflict with other constructs (Hi'), so prefer "each Hi is..." or invent other names; use apostrophe for possessive ('Hi's descendants').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep symbol notation elegant and avoid crowding pages with many similar symbols; be careful with punctuation and apostrophes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give simple, practical rules rather than optimal-but-complex ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer giving simple rules (e.g., omit an unnecessarily complicated condition) rather than always presenting an optimal but complex formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity aids reader comprehension; provide optimal results separately if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using results before they are proved
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't cite a lemma or theorem that is proved later in the book without making the ordering clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure proof structure respects necessary ordering so the reader can't suspect circular reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ties (nonbreaking spaces) to prevent harmful line breaks in TeX
rubrics_metrics.description: Put ties after words where a line break would interrupt or distort the message (e.g., after 'dominates' in 'v dominates x and x dominates w', or between 'e' and 'is').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain readability by preventing undesirable line breaks; use TeX features to control breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence examples to build on each other
rubrics_metrics.description: Present a sequence of examples that build upon one another rather than many unrelated ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A progressive sequence conveys conceptual development more effectively than isolated examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch formatting spacing (e.g., space before parentheses/brackets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure appropriate spacing in expressions and citations (e.g., '4.3 (below)' not '4.3(below)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small typographic choices affect readability; proof carefully for such spacing issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which vs that: avoid unnecessary 'which' in formal prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Unnecessary use of 'which' where 'that' is correct conveys nervous or unnatural tone on the page; people rarely misuse 'which' in speech but do under pressure in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep text online and search/check for improper 'which' uses; follow Fowler's guidance but be mindful of historical variation.
